title: Largest Palindromic Number
statement:
You are given a string `num` made only of decimal digits. Build a palindrome by choosing at least one of its digits (each digit of `num` can be used at most once, not every digit has to be used) and arranging the chosen digits in any order.

The result must be a valid integer written without leading zeros, so it may start with `0` only if it is exactly `"0"`. Return, as a string, the largest such palindromic integer.
notes:
## Intuition

Among integers without leading zeros, a longer one is always larger, and among equal lengths the one with bigger leading digits wins. A palindrome is a left half, an optional middle digit and the mirrored half. So use as many digit pairs as possible, put the largest pairs on the outside, and then pick the largest leftover digit for the middle. Trying every arrangement of every subset would also work, but only for a handful of digits.

## Approach

1. Count how many times each digit appears in `count`.
2. Build the left `half` from digit 9 down to 0, appending `pairs = floor(count / 2)` copies of each digit and removing those pairs from `count`.
3. Zeros may only go into `half` if a nonzero digit is already there; otherwise the palindrome would start with 0, so stop before digit 0.
4. Choose `middle` as the largest digit with a copy left over (possibly `0`), or nothing.
5. Return `half + middle + mirrored`, where `mirrored` is `half` reversed.

## Example 1, step by step

`num = "444947137"` gives counts `1:1, 3:1, 4:4, 7:2, 9:1`. Going down: digit 7 adds one pair (`half = "7"`), digit 4 adds two pairs (`half = "744"`), and the other digits have no pairs. The largest leftover digit is 9, so `middle = "9"`. The answer is `"744" + "9" + "447" = "7449447"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one counting pass, and the output has at most n characters.
- Space: O(n) for the returned string; the counts take O(1).

## Pitfalls

- An input of only zeros (or zeros plus single unpaired digits) must give `"0"` or that single digit, never `"00"` or `"010"`.
- Zero pairs are fine in the inside of the palindrome once a nonzero pair leads it, as in `"000011"` → `"100001"`.
- The middle digit is chosen after the pairs: a digit that appeared an odd number of times keeps one copy for it.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | how many copies of each digit are still unused |
| `half` | left half of the palindrome, largest digits first |
| `digit` | the digit being considered |
| `pairs` | how many pairs of that digit go into the halves |
| `middle` | optional centre digit |
| `mirrored` | `half` reversed, forming the right side |

narration.2: Ten counters, one for each digit 0 to 9.
narration.4: Count every digit of num; order in num does not matter since digits may be rearranged.
narration.6: The left half of the answer is built outside-in.
narration.7: Visit digits from largest to smallest so bigger digits sit on the outside.
narration.8: Zeros cannot lead the number, so they only join the half after some nonzero digit.
narration.9: Nothing nonzero was paired, so stop instead of producing a leading zero.
narration.11: Each pair puts one copy on the left and one on the right.
narration.12: Append all pairs of this digit to the left half.
narration.13: Those digits are used up; only an odd leftover copy may remain.
narration.16: Look for the largest digit that still has a copy left over.
narration.17: A leftover copy can sit alone in the centre.
narration.18: Use it as the middle digit.
narration.22: The right side is the left half read backwards.
narration.23: Join the three parts into the largest palindrome.
